papers.title: EEG-Based Cognitive Overload-Driven Adaptive Training for Enhancing Performance Under Simulated High-Stress Space Operation Tasks.
papers.abstract: Given the potential for highly complex and high-risk space operation tasks to induce cognitive overload in operators, effective training is crucial for maintaining mission performance and safety. Conventional adaptive training often struggles to balance task challenge while preventing overload. To address this limitation, this study proposes an EEG-based cognitive overload-driven adaptive training method that integrates hybrid feature selection, Normalized Fast Dynamic Time Warping (NFDTW)-based feature alignment and a shared knowledge layer to improve online cognitive overload detection under nonstationary conditions. A dual-factor task regulation strategy combining task performance and cognitive overload states is further developed to adjust task difficulty based on these two factors. The results showed that the proposed detection method achieved online detection accuracies of 92.07% and 84.67% on the two datasets, respectively, with maximum relative improvements of 7.74% and 8.34% over the comparison methods. The adaptive training strategy was further evaluated in a VR-based robotic arm docking task involving three groups: fixed, control, and adaptive. Mixed-design ANOVA showed that the adaptive group exhibited significant improvements in task performance and SAS as well as more favorable changes in EEG features. Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparisons further revealed significant group differences ([Formula: see text]). These findings demonstrate the feasibility of EEG-based cognitive overload-driven adaptive training for complex space operation scenarios.

papers.title: Characterization of Sleep, Spectral, and Epileptiform Activity in Individuals Aged 8-27 Years with SYNGAP1-Related Disorder Using an at-Home Dry EEG Headband
papers.abstract: SYNGAP1-related disorder (SYNGAP1-RD) is associated with sleep disturbances, seizures, and neurophysiological abnormalities. However, in-lab EEG can be difficult to obtain due to the behavioral and sensory disorders associated with this condition. In this study we collected EEG in SYNGAP1-RD participants (n=30 enrolled, 27 contributing data) in a decentralized protocol using a dry electrode headband as a path to longitudinal, research-grade data collection in this population. At-home data collection was successful with 180 recordings containing over 1 hour of usable data collected from 23 participants. Across these recordings, sporadic interictal epileptiform discharges were present in 22 of 23 participants but electrographic seizures were not observed. Relative to an adolescent control population (n=10), SYNGAP1-RD participants showed increased wake after sleep onset, reduced sleep efficiency, and decreased time in N1 and N3 sleep stages along with increased time in N2. We reproduced prior findings from awake spectral EEG analyses, including elevated broadband power along with reduced relative alpha power and alpha-theta ratio in the SYNGAP1 cohort. Notably, differences in spectral power were tightly linked to sleep stage, revealing sleep-stage-dependent spectral biomarker dynamics not previously characterized in SYNGAP1-RD. Finally, we examined differences between variants producing truncations downstream of the GAP domain and those producing truncations before or within it, but analyses were limited by a small sample size (n=4 for the post-GAP variant). Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of at-home multi-night sleep EEG collection in participants with SYNGAP1-RD and led to both corroborative and novel findings.

papers.title: Same pipelines, different answers: how evaluation design shapes EEG seizure prediction
papers.abstract: Seizure-prediction studies on scalp electroencephalography (EEG) often report accuracies that would be clinically useful, yet the score a model receives also depends on how its test data were separated from its training data. We kept five published pipelines fixed, from a spectral baseline (power spectral density with linear discriminant analysis, PSD+LDA) to a transformer, and changed only how they were evaluated on the CHB-MIT database. When whole subjects were held out in 20 repeated partitions, every pipeline scored close to the 0.5 reference (mean area under the ROC curve, AUC, 0.527-0.553), and the five pipelines differed less from one another than each varied between partitions. Within patients, PSD+LDA reached an AUC of 0.815 when windows were allocated at random but 0.572 when each preictal block was kept intact and later seizures were held out for testing. Tracing every window back to its recording showed that an index-based within-patient split had let raw EEG samples cross the train-test boundary in all ten eligible cases. Thresholds tuned to allow 1.67% false positives on validation data did not hold that rate on new subjects, and at those thresholds only 2-6% of preictal windows were detected. A zero-shot test of the baseline on the Siena database gave an AUC of 0.480. In this benchmark, the choice of evaluation changed the answer far more than the choice of architecture. We release the window manifests, partitions and predictions so that new models can be tested on the same terms. All results concern retrospective window classification, not continuous alarms.

papers.title: Cross-Domain Slow Wave Sleep Detection from Single-Lead EEG in Pediatric Congenital Heart Disease Recovery.
papers.abstract: Slow wave sleep (SWS) is vital for neural recovery and cardiovascular stability in children following congenital heart disease (CHD) surgery. However, pediatric CHD sleep patterns are often disrupted by clinical stressors and exhibit substantial domain discrepancies relative to adult data distributions. To address these challenges, this study establishes the Pediatric Cardiac Post-surgical Sleep (PCPS) dataset, a self-collected and expert-annotated pediatric polysomnography (PSG) dataset specifically targeting the early post-CHD surgical period. We further propose PCPS-SleepNet, an end-to-end deep learning framework for cross-domain sleep staging from single-lead EEG, enabling effective knowledge transfer from public sleep data to pediatric post-surgical CHD data. The architecture employs a multi-band input representation across six sub-bands and leverages a Four-Stage Progressive Encoder integrating Multi-Scale Depthwise Convolution (MSDC) for local features, self-attention for global density modeling, and a Conformer block for hybrid refinement. To mitigate limited pediatric data availability and domain shift, this network is pre-trained on public datasets and fine-tuned on the PCPS dataset. Subject-independent validation showed competitive performance, with an overall accuracy of 75.65 ± 0.58%, an AUROC of 89.06 ± 0.18%, an AUPRC of 83.49 ± 0.13%, and a macro F1-score of 76.68 ± 0.70%. For SWS detection, the model achieved an AUPRC of 87.89 ± 0.20% and an F1-score of 81.55 ± 0.74%. Architectural ablations and frequency-band input contribution analysis supported the model design and suggested the complementary discriminative value of slow-wave frequency-band inputs. These results suggest a practical and patient-friendly sleep detection solution for individualized sleep assessment and rehabilitation in vulnerable pediatric populations.

papers.title: Coordinated Drift of Image Representations in Human EEG
papers.abstract: Sensory representations drift over time in many animal systems, but evidence in humans remains limited. Moreover, how perception remains stable despite representational drift remains unclear. Here, we used THINGS-EEG2, a dataset with multiple sessions of repeated presentations of natural images, to test whether image-evoked EEG responses drift across recording sessions and whether this drift is geometrically constrained. We found that image-specific EEG response patterns drifted in a manner that was coordinated across channels and concentrated along dimensions that encoded image identity. Although this impaired cross-session decoding accuracy on average, its effects were heterogeneous with some image pairs becoming harder to distinguish and others becoming more separable. Critically, global distance statistics and the dimensionality of the image response space were preserved across sessions. Simulations show that downstream Hebbian networks can adapt faster to structured drift that preserves dimensionality than when drift is unstructured. These findings suggest that human sensory representations can change over time while remaining amenable to rapid compensation via unsupervised learning mechanisms.

Simulations indicate Hebbian downstream networks adapt faster to such structured drift than to unstructured drift.

papers.title: Capturing Class Differences in EEG Connectivity with Class-discriminative Multivariate IMagInary Coherency (CMIMIC).
papers.abstract: A major challenge in EEG/MEG analysis is to characterize task-dependent functional connectivity in a way that is statistically robust and spatially interpretable, without prior source modeling or region-of-interest selection. Comparing connectivity between conditions is statistically demanding due to the high dimensionality of connectivity estimates, and spatial interpretability is compromised when effects are fragmented across many tests. Here, we introduce Class-discriminative Multivariate ImagInary Coherency (CMIMIC), a multivariate method that maximizes differences in the imaginary part of coherency between two classes, enabling the robust identification of condition-specific functional interactions while minimizing spurious connectivity due to volume conduction. We evaluated CMIMIC using simulations and resting-state EEG data of young and older adults in eyes open and eyes closed conditions. In simulations, CMIMIC recovered both the temporal dependencies between sources and their underlying generating networks. On empirical data, the CMIMIC-based pipeline consistently outperformed those based on traditional imaginary coherence (ImCoh) across classifiers and conditions. All methods performed better with eyes open than closed, but CMIMIC showed only a modest performance drop, in contrast to substantial losses for ImCoh. Feature stability analyses revealed that CMIMIC identifies a core set of informative sources largely shared across conditions, whereas ImCoh features were more condition-specific. CMIMIC also provides spatially interpretable source configurations that align well with known neurophysiological effects, offering a reliable, interpretable, and condition-robust approach for extracting discriminative connectivity features from EEG data.

papers.title: Quantifying Interictal Spike Asymmetry on Scalp EEG to Lateralize the Seizure-Onset Zone in Temporal Lobe Epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Accurate lateralization of the seizure focus in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is critical for surgical planning. Our current approach of capturing multiple seizures often misses bilateral disease because of seizure-onset variability. Interictal spike rate asymmetry is a promising marker of TLE laterality. However, visual analysis has low interrater reliability and cannot estimate long-term spike rates. This study evaluated whether asymmetry of automatically detected interictal spikes on scalp EEG can lateralize the clinician-annotated seizure focus in TLE. We performed a retrospective cohort study of patients with drug-resistant TLE who underwent scalp EEG recording at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania. Spike rates were quantified using a validated deep learning model, with a novel leave-one-hemisphere-out approach developed to lateralize the side of the spikes. We developed a logistic regression model to predict the clinician-determined laterality. Model performance was assessed using the area under the ROC curve (AUC), accuracy, and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC). Of 365 included patients (205 women [56.2%]; median age 38, range 18-86 years), the training cohort comprised 261 patients and the independent, time-shifted validation cohort comprised 104. In the test cohort, classification of left TLE vs right/bilateral achieved an AUC of 0.78 (95% CI 0.69-0.87), an accuracy of 70%, and an AUPRC of 0.80 (95% CI 0.69-0.91), and classification of right TLE vs left/bilateral achieved an AUC of 0.80 (95% CI 0.70-0.88), an accuracy of 75%, and an AUPRC of 0.71 (95% CI 0.56-0.85). Model-surgery concordance was positively associated with favorable surgical outcomes. Engel I outcomes were associated with higher concordance probabilities (median difference = 0.20; 95% CI -0.02 to 0.39; r = 0.35; p = 0.037), and no significant association was observed for ILAE 1-2 (median difference = 0.20; 95% CI -0.06 to 0.38; r = 0.29; p = 0.084). Interictal spike asymmetry on scalp EEG shows promise as a noninvasive lateralizing marker in TLE. Applying this model could confirm TLE laterality when it agrees with other noninvasive data or identify patients with a high likelihood of bilateral TLE, potentially avoiding un-necessary invasive studies and reducing the number of seizures needed for evaluation.

papers.title: Diphenhydramine disrupts sleep architecture in 5XFAD Alzheimer's disease model and wild-type mice.
papers.abstract: Sleep disruption is common in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Diphenhydramine (DPH), a first-generation antihistamine with anticholinergic properties, is widely used as an over-the-counter sleep aid. We tested whether chronic DPH treatment alters sleep architecture in 5XFAD and wild-type female mice. Female 5XFAD (n = 16) and wild-type (WT) littermates (n = 14) were implanted with wireless telemetry recording devices to measure electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG) continuously. After a 24h baseline recording at 5 months of age, mice received oral DPH (10 mg/kg) or vehicle at ZT0 for one month. After this chronic treatment, sleep was recorded continuously for 48h during ongoing dosing. Sleep was scored as rapid eye movement (REM), non-rapid eye movement (NREM) 1, NREM2, or wake. A survival curve analysis was used to investigate the microarchitecture of sleep phases after chronic diphenhydramine treatment. At baseline, 5XFAD female mice had more time in NREM1 than WT female controls and had shorter REM and NREM2 bouts. Chronic DPH treatment fragmented NREM2 in both genotypes, reducing long NREM2 bouts. DPH increased total duration of NREM1 and REM during the active phase, and disrupted the light-dark distribution of sleep. DPH did not rescue 5XFAD sleep deficits; instead, DPH treatment resulted in NREM2 fragmentation. Overall, chronic DPH use degrades sleep quality and increases fragmentation in both WT and AD-model female mice, which questions the use of sedating anticholinergics as sleep aids, especially in AD.

papers.title: A self-supervised reconstruction framework for segment-level detection of task-induced deviations in multi-channel EEG.
papers.abstract: Understanding brain activations during mental arithmetic tasks provides valuable insights into cognitive processing. However, analyses of the same electroencephalogram (EEG) dataset have produced inconsistent findings about the cortical regions involved, raising methodological questions about global signal treatment. Detecting task-related activations without pre-labelled datasets further remains challenging when supervised approaches are not applicable. This study presents a self-supervised framework for segment-based anomaly detection using deep learning to identify EEG signal outliers during mental arithmetic. Using a hierarchical variational auto-encoder, the study reconstructed multichannel EEG data segmented into 1-second intervals and trained exclusively on resting-state recordings. The study assessed reconstruction quality using multiple error metrics, including dynamic time warping, short-time Fourier transform loss, and signal-to-noise ratio, applied individually to channel segments. Outlier segments were detected based on the elevated reconstruction error relative to the resting baseline, using an unsupervised detection method. By analysing deviations at the segment level rather than treating the signal globally, the proposed framework captured transient cortical dynamics that may otherwise be obscured. The results demonstrated that these outlier segments exhibited distinct temporal and spectral characteristics, particularly within the delta, theta, and beta bands, and were most frequently located in peripheral electrodes such as Fp2, O1, O2, P3, and T6. Additionally, co-occurrence analysis uncovered functional patterns of simultaneous anomalies across specific electrode pairs and triplets, suggesting temporally dynamic and spatially distributed cognitive processes during arithmetic reasoning. Overall, the proposed framework provided a fine-grained temporal and spatial characterisation of EEG deviations during mental arithmetic and offers a methodological perspective that helped explain discrepancies in previously reported electrode-level findings.

papers.title: Style transfer mapping with ensemble learning for cross-subject EEG-based neuropsychiatric disease recognition.
papers.abstract: Cross-subject electroencephalogram (EEG) recognition remains a fundamental challenge because large inter-subject variability causes severe distribution shifts that substantially degrade the generalization ability of existing learning models. Most existing transfer learning methods attempt to align global feature distributions but often overlook subject-specific structural variations, resulting in unstable adaptation under limited calibration data. To address this problem, we propose a Prototype-Consistent Style Transfer Mapping (PC-STM) framework for cross-subject neuropsychiatric disease recognition. Unlike conventional domain adaptation methods, the proposed framework models subject discrepancy as a prototype-guided style transformation that explicitly aligns target representations with class-consistent source prototypes while preserving discriminative structures. Specifically, a multi-source prototype construction strategy is introduced to characterize representative class distributions, followed by a confidence-aware transductive semi-supervised style transfer module that iteratively refines transformation parameters using labeled calibration samples and unlabeled evaluation samples. Furthermore, a reliability-aware ensemble learning strategy dynamically aggregates multiple subject-specific classifiers according to their calibration consistency, thereby improving robustness against heterogeneous subject distributions. Experiments on two public EEG datasets covering major depressive disorder and Parkinson's disease show stable performance under the evaluated leave-one-pair-out protocol. The calibration labels are inherited from the public dataset cohorts or task conditions, and the study does not constitute prospective clinical diagnostic validation. Beyond the evaluated EEG tasks, prototype-guided style transfer may provide a basis for future investigation of other limited-supervision recognition problems.

papers.title: A representation-level wavelet-EMD fusion framework for spectral analysis and detection of epileptiform patterns in pediatric EEG: computational validation with a roadmap for external benchmarking.
papers.abstract: Pediatric EEG analysis for epilepsy detection is challenged by the non-stationary and developmentally heterogeneous nature of epileptiform activity. Conventional Fourier approaches provide limited time-frequency localization, whereas single-domain methods such as the wavelet transform and empirical mode decomposition (EMD) each exhibit complementary weaknesses. We developed a representation-level wavelet-EMD fusion framework that integrates wavelet and EMD spectra before feature extraction. The pipeline included adaptive wavelet denoising, energy-criterion EMD, weighted time-frequency fusion, extraction of eight spectral-temporal features, and classification using a soft-voting ensemble of a radial basis function support vector machine, random forest, and neural network. Evaluation was performed on 2,000 synthetic pediatric EEG segments spanning canonical epileptiform morphologies and multiple signal-to-noise ratios. A feature-level fusion variant was implemented as an ablation comparator to isolate the effect of fusion strategy while preserving identical feature extraction, classifier architecture, and validation procedures. Across 10-fold stratified cross-validation with 100 Monte Carlo replications, the proposed framework achieved 94.6 ± 0.6% accuracy, 93.7 ± 0.8% sensitivity, 95.5 ± 0.5% specificity, F1 score of 0.943 ± 0.007, and AUROC of 0.971 (95% CI, 0.962-0.978). Performance exceeded standalone wavelet, EMD, and Fourier baselines (all p < 0.001). Representation-level fusion also outperformed feature-level fusion by 1.4 percentage points in accuracy, with the greatest gains observed for polyspike and slow-wave morphologies. On the synthetic corpus the framework was competitive with EEGNet and a 1D convolutional network while retaining explicit time-frequency interpretability. In an external feasibility validation on the CHB-MIT pediatric scalp EEG corpus (14 subjects, leave-one-subject-out), representation-level fusion attained the highest performance of all methods (AUROC 0.901, accuracy 86.7%), confirming that the fusion strategy transfers to real recordings, with performance decreasing as expected. Representation-level wavelet-EMD fusion provides an interpretable and transparent computational framework for analyzing non-stationary pediatric epileptiform EEG whose advantage over classical time-frequency baselines persists, at feasibility scale, on real CHB-MIT recordings and remains competitive with deep-learning baselines. Because the primary evaluation is synthetic and the external validation is a feasibility-scale demonstration, these figures should be read as evidence of methodological viability and external transportability rather than definitive clinical performance; validation on larger, multi-center and prospective pediatric cohorts is the essential next step.

papers.title: Measuring Sleep at Home in Adolescents With Autism Using EEG Headbands: Protocol for a Remote Study.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are prevalent in autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) and worsen daytime functioning, yet their neural bases remain poorly understood. This may reflect the challenges of laboratory-based polysomnography for individuals with ASD, including sensory sensitivities and difficulty adapting to changes in routine. The advent of wearable electroencephalography (EEG) devices allows for remote data collection in the home and facilitates large-scale sleep studies. The aim of this study is to test the hypothesis that thalamocortical circuit dysfunction contributes to poor sleep in ASD by characterizing sleep oscillations that rely on this circuitry. To achieve this goal, we monitored sleep in the home using wearable EEG headbands in adolescents with ASD, including those who are profoundly affected, and their typically developing peers. When necessary, we used a desensitization protocol to gradually acclimate participants to wearing the headband overnight to promote the inclusion of individuals with sensory sensitivities and high support needs. Participants and their families completed assessments and questionnaires and received remote training to use a wearable EEG headband. Those needing time to acclimate followed a personalized 2-week desensitization protocol with a practice headband. Sleep was monitored at home for 3 consecutive nights, the first of which was for adaptation to the headband. Sleep data quality was checked daily, and remote technical support was provided as needed. Using sleep rhythms as physiological biomarkers of thalamocortical circuit function, we will test the hypothesis that abnormal circuit function in ASD is related to worse sleep quality. This study was funded by the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative (SFARI) and approved by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board in November 2021. Data were collected between July 2023 and November 2025. A total of 146 participants (ASD: n=77; typically developing [TD]: n=65; profound autism: n=4) completed the study and produced at least 1 night of usable sleep data. Data analysis is underway, and the results will be submitted for publication in November 2026. At-home sleep monitoring enables large samples that are needed to characterize the neural underpinnings of sleep disturbances across the autism spectrum. The personalized desensitization protocol promotes inclusion by accommodating individuals often excluded from research due to sensory or behavioral challenges. These methods are adaptable for other conditions and research goals beyond ASD, such as longitudinal studies across development or characterizing sleep in other neurodevelopmental disorders. Desensitization protocols may also increase the tolerability of diagnostic laboratory-based sleep studies and other medical procedures, improving both patient experience and quality of care.

papers.title: A generative framework for estimating brain energy landscapes from continuous neuroimaging observations.
papers.abstract: Pairwise maximum entropy models (pMEMs) are gaining increasing attention as a principled way to study nonlinear brain-state transitions. By representing each brain region as a binary active/inactive state and estimating the least-biased probability distribution over all such network configurations, pMEMs reconstruct an energy landscape in which local minima correspond to stable or metastable brain states and transitions reflect movement across attractor basins. However, neuroimaging recordings are continuous and spatially mixed, forcing conventional pMEM analyses to demean and hard-threshold each channel. This ad hoc binarization discards amplitude information and can conflate spatially correlated noise or source mixing with genuine neural coupling. We introduce a hierarchical generative pMEM that links latent binary network states to continuous observations. Node-specific baseline and gain parameters model amplitude modulation, compound-symmetry noise captures shared residual covariance, and, for electroencephalography/magnetoencephalography (EEG/MEG), the electromagnetic leadfield is included as a generative forward model rather than a preprocessing inverse. Model parameters and latent states are jointly estimated using exact posterior enumeration for the small networks analyzed here and a mean-field extension for larger networks. Controlled simulations demonstrated two complementary advantages of the proposed framework. Residual-covariance modeling improved recovery of pMEM fields, couplings, and latent states by accounting for shared fluctuations, with the clearest gains when residual spatial correlation was sufficiently strong. The generative leadfield model further improved sensor-space inference by avoiding inverse-first source reconstruction, including settings in which covariance modeling alone offered limited gains. Resting-state EEG validation showed higher residual correlation during eyes-closed than eyes-open rest, consistent with elevated and spatially coherent alpha activity. Applied further to propofol sedation EEG (alpha-band amplitude envelopes, 8-13 Hz), the fitted 6-node default mode network (DMN) model showed pipeline-dependent condition effects in residual spatial correlation and basin entropy, not apparent under the conventional demean-based pMEM.

papers.title: Learning Kolmogorov Backward Operators for Spectral Analysis and Forecasting: A Data-Driven Variational Galerkin Framework
papers.abstract: For a time-homogeneous Markov process, the fixed-lag solution operator \( (T_τf)(x)=\mathbb E[f(X_{t+τ})\mid X_t=x] \) of the Kolmogorov backward equation evolves observables linearly and deterministically, even when the dynamics are stochastic. We approximate this operator using a two-stage method where we first approximate this operator directly from data, without knowledge of the governing equation (e.g., Fourier Neural Operator), and then compress the Galerkin projection onto a finite-dimensional observable space that is fixed in advance or selected variationally. The error analysis traces the learning error of the estimator, the sampling error of the Galerkin inner products, and the invariance and reconstruction properties of the observable space to the computed spectra and forecasts. The sampling error enters only through a multiplicative factor. Near an isolated spectral cluster, the invariance defect of a subspace controls its distance from the target invariant subspace. The forecast error is controlled by the one-step error of the reduced model and the projection error of the observable; when the measure is invariant and the reduced model preserves constants and is stable on mean-zero observables, the bound is uniform in the horizon. For deterministic dynamics, a learning rate for Fourier neural operators (FNOs) gives one explicit bound for the learning error. Numerical experiments illustrate spectral approximation and forecasting, including long-rollout stability and a comparison with extended dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD) when fewer transition pairs than basis functions are observed.

papers.title: Detection of Spreading Depolarization with Noninvasive Electroencephalography
papers.abstract: Background and Purpose: Spreading depolarizations (SDs) are waves of near-complete breakdown of the transmembrane ion gradients that underlie migraine aura and occur in patients with moderate-to-severe traumatic, ischemic or hemorrhagic brain injury. SDs are involved in primary and secondary brain injury. They are associated with poor neurological outcome and represent a modifiable therapeutic target. However, despite decades of investigation, SD detection still requires invasive subdural electrocorticography (ECoG) using an implanted subdural electrode strip, restricting monitoring to a small subset of neurosurgical patients. Methods: We developed WAVEFRONT, a noninvasive scalp electroencephalography (EEG) biomarker of SD based on spatiotemporal propagation characteristics of delta-band EEG activity. The biomarker was trained and validated using concurrent, multi-day scalp EEG and invasive subdural electrocorticography recordings from patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI), subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), or malignant hemispheric stroke (MHS) across three institutions. We assessed out-of-sample performance across institutions, diagnosis, and surgical approaches, as well as calibration, temporal synchrony, and spatial specificity relative to gold-standard SDs annotated on ECoG. Clinical utility was further evaluated in 607 patients comatose after cardiac arrest from the multicenter International Cardiac Arrest REsearch (I-CARE) consortium, a population in whom invasive monitoring is not performed. Outcome analyses excluded patients who died (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 5) because death may reflect decisions to withdraw life-sustaining treatment in addition to neurological injury. Results: A total of 1,119 gold-standard SDs were annotated in 32 patients (TBI, n=17; SAH, n=12; MHS, n=3; range 0-187 SDs per patient). Across exhaustive cross-validation and institution-, diagnosis-, and surgical approach-based hold-out analyses, WAVEFRONT models trained on one set of patients consistently maintained high performance when evaluated in previously unseen out-of-group cohorts. At the optimal operating point, WAVEFRONT achieved a mean cross-validated true positive rate of 97.3+/-1% with a false positive rate of 6.0+/-0.5%, calculated over 2-min sliding windows with 30-s overlaps. The cumulative duration of WAVEFRONT detections within 30-hour windows strongly correlated with the number of SDs measured by invasive ECoG (R^2=0.7411). Scalp-detected depressions were spatially consistent with the location of the invasive recording strip, and visual inspection demonstrated close temporal correspondence with invasive detections, including during SD clusters. External validation in the independent I-CARE cohort using WAVEFRONT trained on the invasive-monitoring cohort demonstrated significantly greater SD burden on day 3 of post-arrest EEG monitoring among patients with poor neurological outcome (CPC 3-4, n=29) than those with good outcome (CPC 1-2, n=225; p=0.007). Conclusions: Eight decades after Leao's description of SD in 1944, we propose and validate a noninvasive scalp EEG biomarker of SD. Consistent performance across institution-, diagnosis-, and surgical approach-based hold-out analyses, together with burden calibration, spatial specificity, and temporal synchrony with ECoG detections, supports the validity of the WAVEFRONT framework. The association of biomarker burden with neurologic outcome after cardiac arrest suggests that noninvasive monitoring may enable investigation of spreading depolarizations in populations where invasive monitoring is not feasible. Future studies should evaluate prospective performance, treatment responsiveness, and disease-specific associations of the SD biomarker with clinical outcome.

papers.title: Towards improving Alzheimer's intervention: a machine learning approach for biomarker detection through combining MEG and MRI pipelines.
papers.abstract: To identify robust biomarkers for early cognitive decline, classification performance was evaluated for healthy controls (HC) versus mild cognitive impairment (MCI) using MEG-derived spectral features at the sensor and source levels, and by testing whether adding MRI anatomical features improves discrimination in the BioFIND cohort. Data from 324 participants (166 HC and 158 MCI) were analyzed using automated artifact rejection and source reconstruction. Spectral biomarkers, including sensor-space and sourcespace representations, were extracted from the magnetometer and gradiometer signals. Five inverse-solution methods were assessed (including linearly constrained minimum variance [LCMV] and exact low-resolution electromagnetic tomography analysis [eLORETA]) to increase the robustness of source-based biomarker selection. Multiple classifiers, including a support vector machine (SVM) and L1-regularized logistic regression (GLMNET), were compared using nested K-fold cross-validation embedded in Monte Carlo replications to limit overfitting. The best performance was obtained by combining MRI features with source-based MEG features using GLMNET, achieving 76.31 ± 1.47% accuracy and 82.44 ± 1.44% AUC. MEG-only models showed strong discrimination and outperformed MRI-only analyses, particularly those based on the LCMV and eLORETA features. Across settings, the SVM and GLMNET were the most consistently effective classifiers. These findings support MEG/EEG spectral biomarkers, particularly source-based representations, as sensitive markers of early AD-related functional changes. Integrating MEG with MRI can further improve HC-versus-MCI classification. The study also demonstrated that rigorous validation (nested cross-validation with Monte Carlo replication) is essential for reliable biomarker assessment and for comparing preprocessing, inverse-solution, and classifier choices in translational neuroimaging pipelines.

papers.title: GeoMind: Dancing with Geometric Brain Rhythm on Symmetric Positive Definite Manifolds.
papers.abstract: State space model (SSM) is a powerful tool in neuroscience field to characterize the dynamic nature of brain functions by elucidating the mechanism of how brain system transits between brain states and how underlying states give rise to the observed neural activities. Although tremendous efforts have been made to lend the power of deep learning and mathematical insight of SSM in various functional neuroimaging studies, current state-of-the-art methods lack a holistic view of brain state evolution as a self-organized dynamical system where each part of the brain is functionally inter-connected. Since the topological co-activation of functional fluctuations exhibits an intrinsic geometric pattern (symmetric and positive definite, SPD) on the Riemannian manifold, the call for understanding how a selective set of functional connectivities in the brain supports diverse behavior and cognition emerge a new machine learning scenario of manifold-based SSM for largescale functional neuroimages. To that end, we propose a geometric neural network of SSM, coined GeoMind, designed to uncover evolving brain states by tracking the trajectory of functional dynamics on a high-dimensional Riemannian manifold of SPD matrices. GeoMind demonstrates promising results in identifying specific brain states on task-based functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) data, as well as in diseases early diagnosis for Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and Autism, by using resting-state fMRI. These results highlight the applicability of GeoMind in neuroscience research. To further evaluate generalizability of GeoMind, we applied GeoMind to electroencephalography (EEG) emotion datasets, outperforming competing methods and demonstrating scalability across neuroimaging modalities.

papers.title: Mental replay rescales the subjective duration of past events via alpha and theta oscillations
papers.abstract: Human memory recall is flexible in time, allowing past events to be mentally replayed at variable speeds. However, it remains unclear whether temporally rescaled replay distorts the perceived duration of remembered events, and whether such distortion is tied to changes in the retrieved content. Here we instructed participants to mentally replay previously encoded naturalistic videos at compressed, expanded, or self-paced (free) speeds while recording scalp electroencephalography (EEG). Replaying an event at an expanded pace lengthened participants' subsequent judgments of its original duration relative to free and compressed replay, and the longer an event had been replayed, the longer it was judged to have lasted. Crucially, recalled memory content was unaffected, with gist accuracy and recalled detail comparable across speed conditions. During replay, alpha and theta power were reduced under compression, and both interacted with the speed instruction in predicting reported duration. Specifically, alpha power exhibited a stronger positive relationship with duration judgments under compressed replay than under free or expanded replay. Conversely, the relationship between theta power and reported duration was significantly more positive under expanded replay than under free or compressed replay. Neural pattern similarity between instructed and later spontaneous replay varied with replay speed, yet this reinstatement neither predicted reported duration nor mediated the oscillatory effects. These findings suggest that remembered duration is not read out from the amount of content retrieved but reconstructed at retrieval through oscillatory dynamics, decoupling the subjective scaling of time from the content of memory.

papers.title: Beyond Static Representations: Learning Electroencephalogram Spatiotemporal Dynamics for Enhanced Emotion Recognition.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalogram (EEG)-based emotion recognition plays a pivotal role in brain-computer interfaces and mental health monitoring. However, conventional approaches often neglect the intrinsic spatial correlations among EEG channels and fail to effectively model both global temporal dependencies and the continuity of neural oscillations. To overcome these challenges, we propose the Dynamic Spatial Embedding and Temporal Attention Mamba (DSE-TAM) framework. Our Dynamic Spatial Embedding (DSE) module leverages graph convolutional networks to dynamically capture inter-channel relationships, preserving spatial coherence in EEG representations. Subsequently, the Temporal Attention Mamba module integrates self-attention with state-space models to jointly optimize long-range temporal dependencies and smooth transition dynamics. Extensive experiments on 2 public benchmarks (DEAP and DREAMER) and an in-house CEED dataset demonstrate that DSE-TAM surpasses state-of-the-art methods, achieving accuracies of 79.75% (arousal) and 78.27% (valence) on DEAP, 80.55% (arousal) and 83.91% (valence) on DREAMER, and 73.75% (3-class) on CEED. These results validate the framework's efficacy in advancing EEG-based emotion decoding for brain-computer interfaces. The source code is available at https://github.com/Raizeroko/DSE-TAM.

papers.title: Replacing EEG with peripheral physiological signals for driving behavior recognition: a physiology-informed multimodal approach.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) has been widely used for driving behavior recognition due to its ability to capture neural activity; however, EEG acquisition typically requires expensive hardware and complex instrumentation, which limits its practicality in real-world applications. This study investigates whether low-cost peripheral physiological signals can serve as an effective alternative to EEG for driving behavior recognition. A publicly available multimodal driving dataset collected in a simulator environment was analyzed, containing physiological recordings from 35 participants performing five driving behaviors, including smooth driving, acceleration, deceleration, lane change, and turning. Three peripheral physiological signals-electrocardiography (ECG), electromyography (EMG), and galvanic skin response (GSR)-were integrated using a physiology-informed multimodal learning framework designed to capture complementary physiological responses and temporal dynamics across modalities. Experimental results show that the proposed peripheral multimodal configuration (ECG+EMG+GSR) achieves an average accuracy of 0.795 and macro-F1 score of 0.805 under five-fold cross-validation, with MCC and Cohen's kappa reaching 0.731 and 0.730, respectively. Controlled comparisons with six representative baseline methods further showed that the proposed framework consistently outperformed all competing methods across different physiological modality configurations. Notably, the ECG+EMG+GSR configuration outperformed the EEG-only setting while avoiding EEG acquisition and its associated multi-electrode setup, thereby providing strong recognition performance with substantially lower sensing burden and deployment complexity. These findings highlight the potential of multimodal peripheral physiological sensing as a practical and cost-efficient alternative to EEG for driving behavior recognition in intelligent transportation systems.

papers.title: Bridging Sensory Extraction and Decision Dynamics: Face Pareidolia Emergent from Bottom-Up and Top-Down Interactions
papers.abstract: Face pareidolia-the illusory perception of faces in everyday objects-provides a unique window into how the human brain resolves visual ambiguity. Whether pareidolia arises from bottom-up sensory processing or top-down, expectation-driven feedback, is currently debated. Here we recorded electroencephalography (EEG) while participants viewed rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) streams of images, each of which was an object-to-face morph generated along a 21-image continuum via text-to-image diffusion models. Time-resolved representational similarity analyses revealed a clear spatiotemporal dissociation, in which early occipitotemporal areas tracked physical feature changes linearly, while later frontocentral channels collapsed this structural gradient into a sharp, sigmoidal profile reflecting discrete categorical decisions (face-like versus object-like). To characterise information transmission between these regions, we implemented a novel transformation-based representational connectivity analysis. These analyses uncovered an initial feedforward flow of information that transferred and transformed posterior linear traces into anterior sigmoidal representations. Crucially, partitioning the image continuum revealed that unambiguous stimuli (faces or objects) were predominantly resolved via feedforward information flow, whereas ambiguous pareidolic images recruited prolonged top-down feedback. Furthermore, perceptual decision sensitivity was biased by animacy priors and directly predicted individual behavioural reaction times during the task. Together, the findings help reconcile prior debate by establishing that face pareidolia is neither a feedforward process nor an isolated top-down projection, but an active, multi-stage recurrent process driven by feedforward feature extraction and top-down categorical resolution.

papers.title: Resting-state EEG functional connectivity changes following memantine administration in children with autism spectrum disorder: an exploratory pre-post study.
papers.abstract: Despite the widespread use of memantine in modulating excitatory/inhibitory balance, the precise changes in the topology of brain networks following memantine administration in preschool children remain clearly undefined. The objective of this study is a quantitative evaluation of brain functional connectivity changes associated with memantine administration in using EEG-based network analysis. In this research, 22 preschool ASD children underwent treatment with memantine for one month. Resting-state electroencephalogram (EEG) signals were recorded before and after the intervention. functional connectivity matrices were extracted using the Phase Locking Value (PLV) index. Individual-level analysis revealed a Neurophysiological heterogeneity pattern, consisting of a 64% Subgroup with increased network integration (n = 14) with increased connectivity and 36% with decreased connectivity. SPN analysis identified distinct spatial components of network reorganization: (1) localized connectivity suppression in the fronto-central (Fz, F3) and left occipital (O1) regions captured by lower-order spatial filters, and (2) reinforcement of long-range functional coupling and enhanced nodal centrality in the right parietal (P4) and left temporal (T3) regions in higher-order filters. These findings suggest spatial network reorganization patterns associated with memantine administration, characterized by a complementary balance between localized phase decoupling and long-range functional integration.

papers.title: Outcome-Blind EEG Microstate Topography After Cardiac Arrest: Spatial Expression of a Lateralized Microstate and Association with Neurological Outcome.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is central to neurological assessment after cardiac arrest, yet conventional approaches predominantly characterize amplitude, frequency content, continuity, suppression, reactivity, or predefined pathological patterns. EEG microstates provide a complementary framework by describing quasi-stable configurations of the global scalp electric field. We investigated whether an outcome-blind microstate decomposition of EEG from comatose survivors of cardiac arrest identifies reproducible spatial states associated with neurological outcome. We performed a secondary analysis of the multicenter I-CARE/PhysioNet database. Following prespecified EEG screening requiring continuous 19-channel recordings of at least 300 s, 567 subjects were included (34 excluded at preflight). Microstate reconstruction was performed outcome-blind using a fixed 300-s continuous baseline analysis window, GFP-peak sampling capped at 500 peaks per patient, and polarity-invariant clustering across K = 2-10. After model-order evaluation, the K = 4 solution was frozen and backfitted at the patient level. Associations between microstate metrics and neurological outcome were evaluated using unadjusted, multivariable, dose-response, ROC discrimination, and extensive resampling analyses. The primary outcome analysis included 567 patients: 209 with favorable (CPC 1-2) and 358 with unfavorable (CPC 3-5) neurological outcomes. M2 global explained variance (GEV) was higher in patients with favorable outcome (median 0.0852 vs. 0.0564; rank-biserial correlation = 0.185; p = 0.000243; false-discovery-rate [FDR]-adjusted p = 0.000568 within the four-state GEV family). M2 GEV was inversely associated with CPC severity (Spearman rho = -0.144; p = 0.000583; FDR-adjusted p = 0.001419). Standalone ROC analysis yielded an AUC of 0.59 (95% CI 0.54-0.64). After adjustment for age, sex, and shockable rhythm in the extended cohort without return-of-spontaneous-circulation (ROSC) time (N = 535), each 1-SD increase in M2 GEV was associated with greater odds of favorable outcome (OR 1.30, 95% CI 1.07-1.58; p = 0.0092). In the complete-case model additionally adjusted for ROSC time (N = 292), the association remained significant (OR 1.47, 95% CI 1.10-1.97; p = 0.0087). A graded association was observed across M2 GEV quartiles without evidence of nonlinearity. Results remained directionally stable under winsorization, exclusion of distributional extremes, heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors, bootstrap resampling, leave-one-out analysis, repeated leave-five-out perturbations, and accounting for recording-center clustering. By contrast, M2 coverage, mean duration, and occurrence were not significantly associated with outcome after multiplicity correction. An outcome-blind decomposition of EEG after cardiac arrest identified a frozen microstate, M2, whose GEV was reproducibly associated with neurological outcome. The prognostic information associated with M2 was related primarily to the degree to which this spatial configuration explained the global EEG field rather than to its conventional temporal parameters. EEG microstate architecture may provide a complementary description of residual large-scale electrophysiological organization after hypoxic-ischemic brain injury. Rather than functioning as a standalone prognostic test, M2 GEV reflects residual spatial organization that complements established clinical and background EEG markers.

papers.title: E-MDD: an evidence-guided explainable framework for EEG-based depression recognition.
papers.abstract: An evidence-guided explainable framework, E-MDD, is developed to integrate high-dimensional EEG representations, neurophysiological biomarkers, and large language models for the recognition of EEG-based depression with concise and evidence-based textual explanations. The proposed E-MDD framework consists of three stages: classification, evidence construction, and evidence-guided inference. In the classification stage, two parallel feature extraction branches are employed to extract Electroencephalography latent features and neurophysiological biomarkers, which are subsequently fused and fed into a lightweight multilayer perceptron for the recognition of depression. In the evidence construction stage, the latent feature dimensions of the EEG are aligned with neurophysiological biomarkers, and the model's decision basis is identified to construct structured evidence supporting the classification results. In the evidence-guided inference stage, structured evidence and the proposed evidence-guided prompt are used to guide the large language model in generating concise textual explanations. The experimental results on the Mumtaz dataset show that E-MDD achieves an AUC of 0.8472 and an F1-score of 0.8421. Meanwhile, the generated short-text explanations can effectively describe the basis of the model's decision-making for its predictions, demonstrating a high degree of faithfulness. The proposed framework also demonstrates consistent evidence-guided explanation performance across EEGNet and EEGConformer. Overall, this study proposes a neurophysiologically interpretable framework for EEG-based deep learning models, which effectively enhances the interpretability of deep learning models for depression detection and provides a new perspective for understanding their decision-making mechanisms.

papers.title: EEG-based brain effective and functional connectivity predict PET-defined amyloid positivity in cognitively normal individuals.
papers.abstract: Early identification of amyloid-beta (Aβ) pathology is essential for timely intervention in Alzheimer's disease (AD), as Aβ accumulation precedes clinical symptoms by years. We predicted positron emission tomography (PET) -defined Aβ status in cognitively normal individuals using non-invasive resting-state dry electroencephalography (EEG). Brain effective and functional connectivity were quantified to characterize dynamic information transfer between regions. Features derived from dynamic brain connectivity were used to train machine learning models for Aβ classification. EEG-based models can predict amyloid positivity with accuracy comparable to, or in some cases exceeding, that of plasma p-tau217 and previously reported predictors based on cognitive measures, demographics, and health factors, depending on the model. Beyond near real-time Aβ inference, the framework identifies the most affected brain regions and connections associated with neurodegeneration, offering complementary information to blood-based biomarkers and supporting its potential as an affordable tool for early AD detection in primary care and population screening.

papers.title: Electroencephalography Alpha-Band Oscillations as Potential Indicators of Executive Subcomponents Dysfunction correlating to the Severity of Cerebral Small Vessel Disease.
papers.abstract: Cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) relates to executive dysfunction. While electroencephalography (EEG) alpha-band oscillations are promising biomarkers for cognitive impairment, their relationship with specific subcomponents of executive function in CSVD remains unclear. We aimed to investigate the association between EEG alpha-band oscillations and subcomponents of executive function-inhibitory control and working memory-among patients with CSVD. This was a cross-sectional analysis of an ongoing national registry research of CSVD (KY 2019-140-01). Five-minute resting-state EEG was recorded for analyzing occipital and frontal alpha-band indexes including peak frequency (PFα), occipital-frontal ΔPFα, and neurophysiological cognitive level. Inhibitory control and working memory were respectively evaluated by the Victoria Stroop Test (VST) and Digit Span. Associations and screening performance were assessed through logistic regression and ROC-AUC analysis with bootstrap internal validation. A total of 181 CSVD patients (age=60±12.0 years, male=61.9%) were recruited. After adjusting for age, gender, education, and CSVD severity, all PFα were associated with VST trial-2 completion time and VST composite time, respectively (all p<0.05). PFα(O1) have shown association with VST trial-3 completion time (p<0.05). PFα(O1) and PFα(O2) were associated with the high interference score, respectively (all p<0.05). We have set up fifty-six alpha-band-related models, and twenty-four models were selected with apparent AUC ranging from 0.6 to 0.83. The highest apparent AUC for inhibitory control impairment was 0.83, with an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.80. Alpha-band oscillations showed no robust association with working memory. In conclusion, resting-state EEG alpha-band parameters were associated with inhibitory control, but had no connection with working memory, in patients with CSVD. These findings suggested that resting-state EEG alpha-band oscillations can serve as an objective, accessible tool for assessing specific executive deficits in patients with CSVD.

papers.title: Federated Spiking GANs with Rényi Differential Privacy for privacy-preserving synthetic EEG generation in brain-computer interfaces.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) data used in brain-computer and brain-machine interfaces (BCI/BMI) contain sensitive, user-specific information, creating privacy risks in consumer applications such as gaming, human augmentation, and virtual reality. Existing methods like encryption and anonymization either fail to protect data during analysis or still expose identifiable attributes. While differential privacy (DP) offers formal protection, it often reduces data utility. The key challenge is to generate synthetic EEG data that protects sensitive attributes while retaining temporal features for downstream use. To address this, we developed a federated spiking generative framework that integrates a spiking neural network (SNN)-based generator, temporally correlated noise, an artificial neural network (ANN)-based discriminator, and Rényi differential privacy (RDP) within a federated learning framework. The SNN-based generator captures temporal characteristics, and the ANN-based discriminator maintains classification accuracy. Federated training prevents centralization of raw client data, while privacy is preserved through controlled perturbation of spike-train and membrane-potential representations, supported by RDP-based privacy accounting. We evaluated our architecture against methods such as RDP-TimeGAN, RDP-CRNN-GAN, RDP-RCGAN, and RDP-Clare-GAN, demonstrating that our approach preserves temporal features and downstream utility while maintaining privacy in synthetic EEG generation. This solution enables privacy-preserving generation of distributed synthetic EEG data for BCI/BMI research and development.

papers.title: Spectral power and functional connectivity of resting EEG in people exposed to armed conflict and controls
papers.abstract: Exposure to armed conflict can leave persistent effects on mental health, yet its neurophysiological correlates remain poorly characterized, particularly in populations exposed to prolonged violence outside narrowly defined post traumatic stress disorder samples. Here we examined resting state electroencephalographic activity in 122 Colombian adults, including 74 participants exposed to armed conflict and 48 controls. Eyes closed EEG was analysed for 240 seconds per participant. We quantified absolute and relative spectral power across delta, theta, alpha and beta bands and regional functional connectivity using weighted phase lag index in theta, alpha and beta. Group comparisons were adjusted for age, education, sex and assessment year, with correction across 78 EEG contrasts. Median occipital and global alpha power was lower in exposed participants, although adjusted estimates were close to the null and confidence intervals were broad. Temporal theta relative power was lower in exposed participants at nominal significance, but this association did not survive Holm correction. No spectral power or regional connectivity contrast remained significant after multiple testing correction. Exploratory associations between EEG measures and MoCA performance were modest in participants with confirmed scores. These findings provide a systematic characterization of resting EEG after exposure to armed conflict in a population shaped by prolonged violence and displacement. They also indicate that large or widespread alterations in resting spectral power and connectivity were not detectable with the current sample and analytical framework, while defining candidate signals and methodological priorities for larger studies of conflict related brain health.

papers.title: Naturalistic language assessment and brain-network biomarkers in post-stroke aphasia for precision neurorehabilitation.
papers.abstract: Advances in naturalistic language assessment, portable neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and brain-network modeling are creating new opportunities to evaluate post-stroke aphasia under conditions closer to real-world communication. Conventional aphasia batteries and isolated linguistic tasks remain essential for diagnosis, severity classification, and treatment planning, but they provide limited information about how language-network activity supports communication in dynamic, naturalistic contexts. This integrative review, informed by a structured literature search and descriptive thematic mapping, synthesizes evidence on connected speech, discourse production, narrative comprehension, interactive communication, and contextual reading after stroke. We examine how multilevel features from these behaviors can be organized into graded, interacting dimensions of lexical-semantic access, phonological encoding, grammatical organization, discourse processing, executive-predictive control, and speech-motor output. We further review multimodal evidence from fNIRS, fMRI, EEG/ERP, lesion-symptom mapping, structural connectivity, and functional connectivity, highlighting residual left-hemisphere language networks, conditional right-hemisphere support, bilateral reorganization, domain-general control systems, and longitudinal recovery. Portable EEG and fNIRS are considered complementary approaches for repeated assessment during less constrained language tasks, with distinct temporal, spatial, and practical trade-offs. Building on this evidence, we propose an operational ecological biomarker framework that links task choice, multilevel feature extraction, multivariate behavioral profiles, neural measures, prespecified clinical questions, and longitudinal outcomes. This framework may support recovery prediction, rehabilitation stratification, neuromodulation target selection, individualized therapy planning, and monitoring of functional communication.

papers.title: EEG decodability of facial expressions and their stereoscopic depth cues in immersive virtual reality
papers.abstract: Face perception typically occurs in three-dimensional space, where stereoscopic depth cues enrich the perception of facial features. Yet, most neurophysiological research on face processing relies on two-dimensional displays, potentially overlooking the role of stereoscopic depth information. Here, we combine immersive virtual reality (VR), electroencephalography (EEG), and eye tracking to examine the neural representation of faces under controlled manipulations of stereoscopic depth. Thirty-four participants viewed computer-generated faces with neutral, happy, angry, and surprised expressions in frontal view under monoscopic and stereoscopic viewing conditions. Using time-resolved multivariate decoding, we show that EEG signals in immersive VR conditions can reliably differentiate facial expressions. Stereoscopic depth cues elicited a distinct and decodable neural signature, confirming the sensitivity of our approach to depth-related processing. Yet, expression decoding remained robust across depth conditions, indicating that under controlled frontal viewing, the neural representation of behaviorally distinguishable facial expressions is invariant to binocular depth cues. Eye tracking showed that expression-related gaze patterns contained comparable information but did not account for neural representations, while depth information was absent in gaze patterns--consistent with dissociable representational processes. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of EEG-based neural decoding in fully immersive VR as a tool for investigating face perception in naturalistic settings and provide new evidence for the stability of expression representations across depth variations in three-dimensional viewing conditions.

papers.title: Depth-adaptive suppression of subject-dependent interference for robust cross-subject EEG emotion recognition.
papers.abstract: Cross-subject electroencephalography (EEG) emotion recognition is limited by inter-subject variability, which embeds subject-specific nuisance information in learned representations and reduces generalization to unseen individuals. We propose a two-stage layer-adaptive subject-interference suppression framework built on EEG Conformer. In the search stage, differentiable gates and adversarial subject classifiers are attached to hierarchical representations from the patch embedding layer and Transformer blocks to estimate where subject information is most strongly encoded. The top-ranked layers are then fixed and the model is retrained for final emotion classification. A subject-aware supervised contrastive regularizer is further used to improve label-consistent cross-subject representation learning. Experiments on SEED under strict leave-one-subject-out evaluation show improved performance over representative machine-learning, domain-adaptation, and deep-learning baselines. Auxiliary experiments on SEED-IV indicate adaptability under a more challenging label setting. Layer-wise probing shows that subject-specific information remains decodable across depths but is relatively stronger in shallow and early intermediate representations. Selective depth-aware suppression provides a practical and interpretable strategy for robust EEG-based affective brain-computer interfaces.

papers.title: Improvement in naming with tDCS and alteration of functional connectivity in post-stroke aphasia: a randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the effects of anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (A-tDCS) over the left Sylvian parietal temporal region (SPT) on picture naming and auditory comprehension, as well as changes in brain functional connectivity in post-stroke aphasic patients. This is a double-blind, sham-controlled, randomized controlled study. Sixty aphasic patients were randomly assigned to receive either active or sham tDCS over the SPT as well as speech-language therapy for four weeks. Standardized aphasia assessments and electroencephalogram (EEG) examinations were conducted before and after the treatment. The EEG nonlinear index of cross approximate entropy (C-ApEn) was used to assess brain functional connectivity. The tDCS group demonstrated significantly greater improvements than the control group in both picture naming and auditory word-picture identification scores (p < 0.001). Regression analysis revealed that the group (tDCS/control) was the primary factor associated with improving picture naming. The functional connectivity of F3-P3, F7-P3, T3-T5, T5-P3, T5-C3, T4-T6, T3-T4, and T5-T6 significantly increased following tDCS. Anodal tDCS over the left SPT can improve picture naming and auditory comprehension in subacute post-stroke aphasia. Potential mechanisms include enhanced connectivity within the left-hemisphere dorsal/ventral streams, the executive control network, and between the bilateral temporal lobes. These functional connectivity changes provide neural evidence for the effect of tDCS on naming improvement. Clinical trial registry number ChiCTR-TRC-14005072.

papers.title: Assessment of the duration of continuous EEG monitoring in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) can detect seizures and delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) in patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH). Because a standard duration of continuous EEG monitoring to capture these complications has not been established in aSAH, we compared a standard 6- or 7-day cEEG monitoring protocol versus longer periods of monitoring. We performed a retrospective analysis of aSAH patients ≥18 years old grouped by standard monitoring protocol (6-7 days, group 1) and those with longer monitoring (>7 days, group 2). Clinical characteristics, EEG features, length of stay (LOS) and functional outcome were compared using univariate analyses. Multivariable analyses tested the association between the groups and vasospasm, DCI, LOS, and modified Rankin Scale (mRS). 19 patients met criteria for group 1 and 16 patients for group 2. We found no difference in EEG's detection of worsening abnormal EEG activity, vasospasm and DCI. ICU and hospital LOS in group 2 were nearly double that of group 1 (ICU: 25.5 (19.5-35) vs. 14 (11-21) days, p = 0.0003; hospital: 32.5 (29.5-48) vs. 18 (13-29) days, p = 0.003). Good outcome (mRS ≤2) at discharge and at 6 months was similar in both groups (21.1% vs. 0% and 56.3% vs. 46.2%). In multivariable analysis, EEG duration was independently associated with ICU and hospital LOS but not with vasospasm, DCI, and mRS at 6 months. Longer EEG monitoring correlated with significantly longer ICU and hospital LOS but not with vasospasm, DCI, and functional outcome at 6 months. Larger studies to confirm our findings are warranted.

papers.title: Impact of burst suppression duration on delirium and its diagnostic value in mechanically ventilated ICU patients.
papers.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) delirium affects up to 50% of mechanically ventilated patients. This condition is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Although bispectral index (BIS) monitoring is widely used for sedation assessment, its predictive value for delirium remains limited. Burst suppression (BS) is an electroencephalographic pattern reflecting profound cerebral dysfunction. BS has been proposed as a predictor of delirium. However, the quantitative role of burst suppression duration (BSD) in delirium risk stratification has not been established. This prospective observational study enrolled 300 mechanically ventilated adult ICU patients between April 2021 and October 2024 at Harrison International Peace Hospital. Continuous video-electroencephalogram (vEEG) monitoring was performed. BSD was quantified from the vEEG recordings. Delirium was assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU (CAM-ICU). Multivariate logistic regression was used to identify independent risk factors. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of BSD. Among 300 patients, 130 (43.3%) developed delirium. The delirium group had significantly longer BSD than the control group (median 81.1 s, IQR 41.5-148.5 vs. 17.2 s, IQR 5.8-32.9; P < 0.001). Multivariate analysis identified BSD (adjusted OR = 1.018, 95% CI 1.012-1.023; P < 0.001), BIS (adjusted OR = 0.964, 95% CI 0.946-0.982; P < 0.001), age (adjusted OR = 1.024, 95% CI 1.002-1.047; P = 0.031), and hypertension (adjusted OR = 1.748, 95% CI 1.002-3.051; P = 0.049) as independent risk factors. ROC analysis demonstrated that BSD achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.871 (95% CI 0.829-0.913). The optimal cutoff of 41.5 s yielded a sensitivity of 80.8% and a specificity of 78.2%. The combination of BSD and BIS improved the AUC to 0.914 (95% CI 0.882-0.946). BSD is an independent risk factor for delirium in mechanically ventilated ICU patients. It demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy as a quantitative biomarker. The combination of BSD and BIS provides superior predictive performance. This combined approach offers a practical quantitative tool for early delirium risk stratification.

papers.title: General information reliability, perceived educational quality, and transparency of YouTube videos on epileptiform discharges: an exploratory cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is central to diagnosing and classifying epileptiform discharges, but interpretation requires structured training. This exploratory cross-sectional study evaluated general information reliability and completeness, perceived educational quality, and transparency of English-language YouTube videos on epileptiform discharges. Although these patterns are described using established electrographic criteria, interpretation may vary, particularly in borderline recordings. A cross-sectional YouTube search was conducted in May 2025 using five keywords. The first 100 results per keyword were screened and 25 of 500 records met all eligibility criteria. The final sample was limited to narrated, English-language videos lasting 1 to 20 min that were returned by the selected search terms and YouTube ranking system. Two neurologists independently rated the videos using DISCERN as a general reliability indicator, the Global Quality Scale (GQS) for educational quality, and the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) criteria for transparency. Exploratory analyses included group comparisons, Spearman correlations, single-measure intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), effect sizes, confidence intervals, and false-discovery-rate-adjusted q values. Six videos (24%) were from academic/educational channels and 19 (76%) from individual healthcare professionals. Mean scores were 52.1 for DISCERN (95% CI 46.7-57.5), 3.86 for GQS (95% CI 3.58-4.14), and 1.98 for JAMA (95% CI 1.69-2.27). Single-measure ICCs were 0.971, 0.655, and 0.816, respectively. Duration was nominally correlated with GQS (ρ = 0.431, p = 0.031) and JAMA (ρ = 0.553, p = 0.004), and DISCERN with GQS (ρ = 0.496, p = 0.012); none remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction (all q ≥ 0.052). Among the small subset of eligible videos, general-purpose instruments suggested moderate-to-good average perceived educational quality and information reliability, whereas transparency was limited. Because DISCERN, GQS, and JAMA are not EEG-specific and no qualitative EEG-accuracy, pedagogical, or learner-outcome assessment was performed, the findings are exploratory. These results should not be understood as estimating the quality of all YouTube material related to EEG or epileptiform discharges, nor do they establish EEG-specific accuracy or educational effectiveness. The evaluated videos should therefore be used only as critically appraised adjuncts to expert-supervised EEG training.

papers.title: Functional brain activity in cancer-related cognitive impairment: a scoping review of EEG studies.
papers.abstract: Cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI) is reported across the cancer trajectory, yet its neurobiological basis remains incompletely understood. Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a temporally precise method for assessing brain activity at rest and during cognitive processing, but its application in CRCI research has not been systematically mapped. This scoping review characterized how EEG has been used to study cognitive functioning in people with cancer, including populations studied, EEG paradigms and analytic approaches employed, and cognitive outcomes assessed. Following PRISMA-ScR guidance, we searched MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Web of Science from inception to February 2025 for studies using EEG to examine cognitive functioning. Sixty articles were included. Most were small and cross-sectional, with publication output increasing markedly after 2015. Task-based event-related potentials, particularly from oddball and attention tasks, were used most frequently, whereas quantitative EEG approaches, including spectral power and connectivity analyses, were less common. In populations with cancers outside the central nervous system (CNS), longer P300 latency and lower amplitude were common, but opposite and null findings also occurred. Evidence from primary CNS and other intracranial tumor populations was sparse. Across cancer contexts, quantitative EEG findings showed limited convergence across articles. Associations between EEG measures and cognitive outcomes were inconsistent and often not tested directly. Overall, EEG provides a complementary approach to investigating cognition in people with cancer, but the evidence remains methodologically heterogeneous. Larger longitudinal studies, more consistent cognitive outcome selection, and closer integration of neural and cognitive measures are needed to establish reproducible findings and evaluate their potential clinical utility. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251084951.

papers.title: Machine learning based on behavioral, fecal and oocyst analyses for chicken coccidiosis diagnosis: A systematic review with exploratory extension.
papers.abstract: In the context of large-scale and intensive poultry farming, avian coccidiosis causes substantial economic losses. Timely and accurate diagnosis is essential for effective control and prevention. However, conventional diagnostic methods, including microscopic examination and molecular assays, are constrained by limited efficiency and a heavy reliance on specialized expertise, rendering them inadequate for real-time, high-throughput diagnosis in modern farming systems. Recent advances in machine learning have demonstrated significant potential in image recognition and early disease detection, particularly for diagnosing coccidiosis based on fecal and oocyst images, positioning this technology as a promising tool for future diagnosis of avian coccidiosis. Despite considerable progress in this area, approaches that rely solely on fecal and oocyst recognition face challenges in early screening. Moreover, limitations in current datasets and models often lead to insufficient generalization under practical farming conditions. Furthermore, although monitoring behavioral and physiological abnormalities could facilitate early detection, research on this aspect remains largely unexplored for avian coccidiosis. To address these gaps, this systematic review with exploratory extension adopts a three-dimensional framework, "behavioral physiology, fecal characteristics, and oocyst morphology" to systematically summarize the current applications and challenges of machine learning in identifying avian coccidiosis, with the aim of clarifying existing research gaps and technical bottlenecks. Finally, to systematically meet the demand for early and efficient diagnosis, this review proposes a conceptual framework for an AI-based surveillance system for chicken coccidiosis that integrates multimodal data across behavioral screening, fecal validation, and oocyst-based analysis encompassing species identification, oocyst counting, sporulation-state classification and viability assessment. This framework will serve as a theoretical foundation for moving the field from laboratory research toward field applications, thereby enabling early, precise, efficient, and intelligent prevention and control of avian coccidiosis.
