papers.title: Assessment of Compliance With the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence Guidance in the Management of Patients Referred Following a First Suspected Seizure: A Retrospective Clinical Audit.
papers.abstract: Introduction A first suspected seizure requires timely specialist assessment and appropriate investigation to establish an accurate diagnosis, identify seizure mimics, assess the risk of recurrence, and provide appropriate safety advice. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidance recommends urgent specialist assessment following a first suspected seizure, alongside appropriate electrocardiography, electroencephalography, neuroimaging, recurrence-risk assessment, and patient safety advice. This audit evaluated adherence to these standards within a first-seizure clinic. Materials and methods A retrospective clinical audit was undertaken on patients referred to a first-seizure clinic from the Emergency Department and Acute Medicine Unit over a three-month period from January to March 2025. Data were obtained from electronic patient records, clinic correspondence, and discharge documentation. Compliance with predefined standards from NICE guidance was assessed. The primary outcome measures were timely specialist assessment, 12-lead electrocardiography, documentation of individualized seizure recurrence risk, timely electroencephalography where clinically indicated, timely neuroimaging where indicated, and documentation of safety-netting and driving advice. Results Sixty-three patient records were initially identified. Ten patients did not attend or were lost to follow-up and were excluded from the final clinical analysis, leaving 53 patients. Five of 53 patients (9.4%) received specialist assessment within two weeks. A 12-lead ECG was documented in all 53 patients (100%), and an individualized seizure recurrence risk assessment was documented in all patients (100%). An electroencephalogram (EEG) was indicated in 17 patients, of whom one (5.9%) underwent EEG within 72 hours; 15 (88.2%) underwent EEG after 72 hours, and one patient did not attend. The mean time to EEG among those who eventually underwent the investigation was approximately 12.5 weeks. Neuroimaging was indicated in 41 patients, of whom 22 (53.7%) underwent imaging within six weeks and 19 (46.3%) underwent imaging after six weeks. Safety-netting, including documentation of driving/Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) advice, was documented in all 53 patients (100%). Conclusion The audit demonstrated high compliance with core assessment and documentation standards but substantial delays in specialist review and time-critical investigations. The greatest gap was in timely EEG access, followed by delays in specialist assessment and neuroimaging. The findings support service-level interventions aimed at improving urgent access to first-seizure assessment and investigations. A repeat audit, following the implementation of targeted interventions, will be important to determine whether pathway changes improve compliance.

papers.title: Three repeated intrathecal injections of allogenic umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stromal cells in autism spectrum disorder: a Phase I clinical trial.
papers.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition of etiology, characterized by deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviors. Despite its growing prevalence, no treatment has yet demonstrated consistent efficacy across the full spectrum of ASD phenotypes. This Phase I, open-label study investigates the safety and feasibility of three repeated intrathecal injections of allogeneic Umbilical Cord Tissue-Derived Mesenchymal Stromal Cells (UC-MSCs) in children diagnosed with ASD. Five children (aged 3-7) with ASD, confirmed by Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders- Fifth Edition (DSM-5) criteria and on stable behavioral and pharmacologic regimens for at least two months, received three intrathecal (IT) injections of 20 × 10⁶ UC-MSCs at one-month intervals. Safety was monitored over six months based on Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE). Preliminary behavioral assessments, including the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS), Autism Treatment Evaluation Checklist (ATEC), and the Behavior Problem Inventory (BPI-S), were conducted at the baseline, one-, two-, four-, and six-month follow-ups. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytokine profiles were measured prior to each injection. Electroencephalography (EEG) and Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) were performed at baseline and the final follow-up. The treatment was safe and well-tolerated with no serious adverse events (SAEs). All participants experienced at least one mild to moderate, transient adverse event (AEs), most commonly fever (5/5) and nausea (4/5). Exploratory behavioral improvements were observed in CARS in all children, while two participants moved from the mild-to-moderate to the non-autistic ranges, and three shifted from the severe to the mild-to-moderate range. Other measures also improved, though the persistence of these improvements was varied. CSF cytokines showed consistent reduction, particularly in TNF-[Formula: see text] and IL-6 levels across participants, confirming the immunomodulatory impact of UC-MSC administration. The EEG findings revealed that the spectral pattern shifted toward a more typical profile in one participant after treatment. This Phase I study showed that three repeated IT injections of UC-MSCs are safe and well-tolerated in children with ASD. Preliminary behavioral and biomarker improvements warrant further study in larger controlled trials. Trial Registration ID: IRCT20200217046526N3.

papers.title: Electrophysiology Team-Administered Conscious Sedation for Pulsed-Field Versus Radiofrequency Ablation in Atrial Fibrillation.
papers.abstract: Pulsed-field ablation (PFA) is emerging as a novel nonthermal alternative. However, PFA is commonly performed under general anesthesia or deep sedation requiring anesthesiologists, which increases resource utilization and limits its widespread application. This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of conscious sedation for PFA administered by the electrophysiology (EP) team, using radiofrequency ablation (RFA) as a comparator. A total of 120 patients with symptomatic, drug-refractory atrial fibrillation were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to the PFA group or the RFA group. We evaluated three key outcomes: (1) intraoperative patient tolerance, assessed using validated scales (Faces Pain Scale-Revised [FPS-R], Likert Scale Questionnaire [LSQ]) combined with intraoperative body movement and cough reactions; (2) procedural efficiency; and (3) procedural safety. The incidence of pain during pulmonary vein isolation was comparable between the two groups (all p > 0.05), whereas FPS-R scores were significantly lower in the PFA group (p < 0.05). No significant difference was observed in movement scores between the two groups (p = 0.452). According to the LSQ analysis, only 1 patient (1.7%) in the RFA group reported dissatisfaction with intraoperative pain management. Cough incidence during PVI was higher with PFA (21.7% [13/60] vs 6.7% [4/60]; p = 0.018). Both total procedure time and left atrial dwell time were shorter in the PFA group. Furthermore, no serious complications were directly related to conscious sedation. In selected low-risk patients, EP team-administered conscious sedation is feasible for PFA, with acceptable intraoperative tolerance and safety while preserving procedural efficiency.
